Architectural Drivers — Personal Finance Tracker

  • Date: 2026-09-06
  • Owner: Roman Tymoshuk
  • Status: reviewed
  • QA model: ISO/IEC 25010:2023
  • Design purpose: greenfield system
  • Stakeholders: stakeholders.md (ST-1 … ST-6)

This register lists everything that shapes the architecture of the Personal Finance Tracker: four business goals, four use cases, five constraints, six quality attribute scenarios, and two architectural concerns. Each driver has its own file, linked from the tables below; start with the prioritised list if you want to know what matters most, or the traceability matrix to see how the drivers connect.

Prioritised driver list (input to ADD / ATAM)

  1. SQA-1 (H,H) — cross-user access rejected + logged; 0 reads
  2. AQA-1 (H,H) — single-AZ failure recovers < 60 s; ≥ 99.5 %/mo
  3. PQA-1 (H,M) — dashboard < 1.5 s @ p95 at 500 concurrent
  4. UC-1 — record a transaction (write load + latency + modifiability hot spot)
  5. UC-2 — monthly dashboard (performance-critical read path)
  6. CON-4 (hard) — encryption in transit and at rest
  7. CON-2 (hard) — one engineer, 3-month MVP

Architecture: Personal Finance Tracker

  • System: Web app for individuals to track income, expenses and savings goals.
  • Date: 2026-09-06
  • Session: personal-finance-tracker-session.md
  • Drivers: ../drivers/README.md

1. Introduction

A mobile-web personal finance tracker. This document is the ADD 3.0 working architecture after iteration 1 (overall structure, security, availability) and iteration 2 (dashboard read path). Drivers: ../drivers/README.md.

2. Context diagram

Diagram

Source: diagrams/context.puml.

Description

A single external dependency at launch: a transactional email provider. Everything else is owned by the system, keeping the SOC 2 (CON-4) surface small.

4. Container diagram

Diagram

Source: diagrams/container.puml.

Description

The API service is the single write path and the single place tenant scoping (SQA-1) is enforced. The Redis read cache serves the dashboard (PQA-1); it is a performance element, not a system of record, so its loss degrades latency but not correctness (AQA-1). A CSV import goes through the Import Queue to the Import Worker, so a 5 000-row file never holds an API request thread (PQA-1, PQA-2). The worker reuses the Data Access module but not yet the tenant guard: ATAM risk R-1, to be closed by ADD iteration 1b.

5. Component and module views

API Service

Diagram

Source: diagrams/component-api.puml.

Description

Every request passes through the Tenant Guard before any service runs, so cross-tenant access (SQA-1) is structurally prevented rather than checked per-endpoint.

Module decomposition

Diagram

Source: diagrams/module-decomposition.puml.

Description

Four layers inside the single deployable; a layer may use only the layer below it, and the four domain modules may not use one another (a cross-domain need is mediated by reporting reading through persistence). The security layer is the one place tenant scoping is applied (SQA-1, ADR-2); the reporting module's report-type registry is what keeps MQA-1 to a one-day change. This is the seed of the Views-and-Beyond module decomposition view.

6. Sequence diagrams

Source: diagrams/sequence-dashboard.puml.

On a cache hit the database is not touched, which is the common path and keeps p95 under the 1.5 s budget (PQA-1). On a miss the API recomputes from tenant-scoped rows and repopulates the cache; a stale cache is bounded by the 15-minute TTL.

7. Deployment diagram

Diagram

Source: diagrams/deployment.puml.

Description

The API runs as stateless replicas spread across two AZs behind the platform load balancer, and the data tier uses managed primary/standby with automated failover — together these meet AQA-1 (single-AZ failure recovers < 60 s) within the CON-3 low-cost-tier constraint. The Import Worker runs on the same platform and scales on queue depth. Redis holds the read cache and the import stream; neither is a system of record.

POST /transactions — full interface spec (the four agreement points)

The one interface UC-1 and SQA-1 both run through, specified per references/interfaces.md:

Agreement pointSpecification
Scopeavailable to the Web App only, via the CDN + Tenant Guard; not exposed to any other actor. The Tenant Guard is the actor for the Transaction Service.
Interaction stylesynchronous request/response over REST + HTTPS (TLS 1.3); idempotency key header so a client retry is safe; no long-poll.
Data representation & structurerequest {amount: integer (minor units), date: ISO-8601 date, categoryId: uuid, note?: string ≤ 280}; response 201 {id: uuid, ...echo}; JSON (matches the SPA's parser; compact; interceptable for debugging). user_id is never in the body — it is taken from the verified JWT.
Error model400 field-level validation errors (nothing written) · 401 missing/expired token · 403 cross-tenant attempt (written to the append-only audit log, alert < 1 min — SQA-1) · 409 duplicate idempotency key · 503 store unavailable → the client is told "saved, syncing" and the write is queued (UC-1 3a).

Events

EventPublisherConsumersDescription
TransactionWrittenTransaction ServiceCache invalidatorTriggers dashboard-aggregate invalidation for the user/month

9. Design decisions

Each significant decision is an ADR in adr/; this table is the log.

DecisionRationale (cite driver IDs)Alternatives discardedADR
Single API service owns all writes and enforces tenant scoping in one middlewareSQA-1 needs one auditable choke point; CON-2 favours few moving partsPer-service authz checks (easy to miss one)ADR-2
Redis cache-aside for dashboard aggregates with 15-min TTLPQA-1 p95 budget; DB alone won't meet it at 500 concurrentMaterialised views (slower to iterate — MQA-1); CDN caching (per-user data)ADR-1
Managed PostgreSQL primary/standby, multi-AZ, automated failoverAQA-1 recovery target; CON-5 mandates PostgreSQL; CON-3 low-cost tier still offers thisSelf-managed HA (CON-2 time), single instance (fails AQA-1)ADR-3
